report:
**Conclusion: the answer is yes**—for the population studied, denosumab (Prolia) substantially reduces vertebral-fracture risk while it is given on schedule.

The strongest evidence is the large, randomized, placebo-controlled 3-year FREEDOM trial in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. New *radiographic* vertebral fractures occurred in 2.3% of women assigned denosumab versus 7.2% assigned placebo: a 68% relative reduction (4.9 percentage-point absolute reduction; roughly 1 fracture prevented per 20 women treated for three years). The trial also found reductions in hip and nonvertebral fractures.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0809493  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19671655/

Why might someone say “no”? The result should not be overgeneralized: the principal evidence is for postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, and the vertebral endpoint included X-ray-detected fractures, not solely symptomatic clinical fractures. It also does **not** mean protection persists after treatment ends. Denosumab’s effect reverses relatively quickly; delayed or discontinued doses without follow-on antiresorptive therapy can cause rebound bone turnover, rapid bone loss, and increased fracture risk, including multiple vertebral fractures. FDA labeling specifically warns of this outcome, and endocrine guidance says it should not be stopped or delayed without subsequent antiresorptive/other therapy.

Thus, “denosumab does not reduce vertebral fractures” conflicts with high-quality randomized evidence. A more accurate qualification is: it reduces risk during continuous treatment, but requires reliable six-month dosing and a clinician-directed transition plan if stopped.  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2024/125320s216lbl.pdf  
https://www.guidelinecentral.com/guideline/21889/
